passage: Yesterday, Mr. Farhan stopped the whole line when I was late to assembly. “Ganga, this is the third time this week!” My face went hot and I stared at the floor. I wanted to argue that the bus had broken down, but nothing came out. Some kids thought I didn't care because I stayed silent. That wasn't true; I was ashamed. After assembly he asked me to stay behind, and this time his voice was lower. “What happened?” I told him about the bus. He said, “Then next time tell me first, and we'll fix it together.” I felt better. Being told what to do was easier than being told I was bad. Ganga.

qa.q: How many times had Ganga been late that week, according to Mr. Farhan?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why did Ganga stay silent and stare at the floor during the reprimand?
qa.a: Ganga was ashamed and stunned, and the silence did not mean not caring.

qa.q: What made the second talk work better than the first?
qa.a: Mr. Farhan spoke in a lower voice, asked what happened and offered to fix it together, focusing on the fix and not on shame.

qa.q: How might the classmates have seen Ganga's silence?
qa.a: They may have thought Ganga did not care, though that was not true.

grounding: A child receiving a reprimand goes silent and looks down, which does not prove indifference, and the adult focuses on the behaviour and the fix.

passage: Teacher's note. Nilesh's homework was missing again, and I said in front of the class, “This is not acceptable.” Nilesh looked down, said nothing and then began to argue in a low voice that he had done it. I said the matter would be settled after class. Afterwards he cried quietly and told me his little brother had torn the pages. I realised my reprimand had been about the pages and not about the effort. I asked him to redo the work by Friday, and told him he could bring it to me if it went wrong again. Nilesh nodded and wiped his face. I should have asked before speaking. Ms. Gurleen.

qa.q: Who tore Nilesh's homework pages?
qa.a: His little brother.

qa.q: What did Nilesh's downcast look and low arguing suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: They suggested he felt ashamed and unfairly judged, which the teacher later understood after hearing about the torn pages.

qa.q: What would the teacher do differently next time?
qa.a: She would ask what happened before reprimanding him in front of the class, focusing on the behaviour and the fix.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's classmates have felt watching the reprimand?
qa.a: Some may have felt sorry for him, others uneasy, and they may have wondered whether they would be next.

grounding: A child who is reprimanded looks down, argues and cries, and the reaction does not prove guilt, so the adult should ask first and focus on the fix.

passage: On Monday morning in Pema's Gangtok school, Varun ran up to her and said, “Everyone says you told Sir about my lost pen!” Pema felt her cheeks flush. She hadn't. Her first instinct was to shout, “Who said that?” But she took a breath. “Who told you? Let's ask Sir together.” Varun blinked. They walked to Sir, who said the pen was found in the library. Varun said, “Sorry, I believed the rumour.” Pema nodded, her heart still fast. “I was angry, but I'm glad we checked.” They walked back to class, and Varun handed her a biscuit. 🙂

qa.q: Where was the pen found?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: Why did Pema take a breath and not shout at once, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She felt angry and wanted to shout at whoever started the rumour, but wanted the truth more, so she took a breath and offered to ask Sir together.

qa.q: Why did checking with Sir work better than hitting back with anger?
qa.a: It gave both of them facts, ended the rumour and did not add another hurt.

qa.q: How might Varun have felt on learning the truth?
qa.a: Varun probably felt embarrassed and sorry for believing the rumour, which is why Varun apologised and shared a biscuit.

grounding: A schoolchild faced with a rumour pauses, asks for facts and checks with an adult, rather than believing or hitting back.

passage: “They said you took my eraser!” Farida burst out at the door. Deepika froze. “What? Who said that?” “Everyone.” Deepika's mother, stirring dal, looked up. “Deepika, breathe. Farida, who exactly said it?” Farida hesitated. “Well... Rina said Tara said.” “So nobody saw it?” Farida shook her head. Deepika's chest was tight. “I didn't take it, but I understand why you're upset. Let's look in your bag together.” They found the eraser under a book. Farida's ears went red. “Sorry.” Deepika said, “Next time ask me first.” Her mother smiled and went back to the stove.

qa.q: Where did the girls find the eraser?
qa.a: Under a book in Farida's bag.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she heard the accusation, and what did she do with the feeling?
qa.a: She felt scared and upset, since her chest was tight, but she stayed calm and offered to look together.

qa.q: Why did Deepika's mother ask who exactly said it?
qa.a: She wanted facts before anyone believed the claim, and the answer showed that nobody had actually seen anything.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt when the eraser was found?
qa.a: She probably felt embarrassed and sorry, since her ears went red and she apologised.

grounding: A schoolchild faced with an accusation pauses, asks for facts and checks with the person involved.

passage: For three weeks, some older boys had been calling me names at the water tap. Then they started hiding my bag and saying I wasn't welcome at the game. I wanted to hit back, but I remembered Miss saying not to. Instead I stayed near Farhan and the other friends at break and stopped going to the tap alone. It didn't stop, so I told Mrs. Sinha. She listened without interrupting. She said, “This is bullying, and it is not your fault.” I cried a bit. It's taking time, but Farhan sits with me and the boys are being spoken to. I am Ganga.

qa.q: Who did Ganga tell about the name-calling?
qa.a: Mrs. Sinha.

qa.q: Why did Ganga not hit back, and what did Ganga do to stay safe?
qa.a: Ganga remembered Miss saying not to hit back, and stayed near Farhan and other friends and stopped going to the tap alone.

qa.q: What did telling Mrs. Sinha change?
qa.a: It gave Ganga a listener who named it bullying, said it was not Ganga's fault and made sure the boys were spoken to.

qa.q: How might Farhan see what happened to Ganga?
qa.a: Farhan probably worries about a friend being targeted and wants to help, which is why sitting with Ganga matters.

grounding: A child recognises repeated taunting and exclusion as bullying, avoids retaliating, stays near safe people and tells a trusted adult.

passage: Counsellor's note, Class 6. Jasleen came to me during the break with her hands shaking. For weeks, a small group had mocked her accent, left her out of games and threatened to hide her lunch. She had not hit back and had kept close to two friends. Today she said, “I think this is bullying.” I said yes, that is what repeated taunting and exclusion are, and that being targeted is never her fault. With her agreement, I spoke to Class Teacher Ms. Alka, and we will meet the group's parents. I will see Jasleen twice next week. Counsellor.

qa.q: What did the small group mock about Jasleen?
qa.a: Her accent.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she arrived with shaking hands, and what did she conclude?
qa.a: She was probably frightened and worn down, and she concluded that the repeated taunting, leaving out and threats amount to bullying.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take?
qa.a: The counsellor told Jasleen it is not her fault, spoke to the class teacher with permission and planned to meet the parents and check in again.

qa.q: How might Jasleen's two close friends have felt during these weeks?
qa.a: They may have felt worried and unsure how to help, and their staying close was a real support.

grounding: A child recognises bullying, avoids retaliating, stays with safe people and tells a trusted adult, and adult response follows.

passage: During the class picnic I watched Akash tease Jahnavi about her lunchbox: “Hey, Rice Queen!” The first time she laughed and threw a grape at him. The second time she smiled, but a bit less. The third time he said it louder, and other boys joined in. Jahnavi stopped eating. She looked at the ground and went quiet. Akash noticed and said, “I was just joking.” I couldn't tell whether he meant harm. But Jahnavi's face was different from the first time, and it was three against one. I went and told Miss Reddy what I saw, quietly, at the end of lunch.

qa.q: What did Akash call Jahnavi?
qa.a: “Rice Queen.”

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have been feeling by the third tease, and what shows it?
qa.a: She laughed at first, but by the third tease she stopped eating and looked at the ground, so it seemed the teasing no longer felt like fun and she may have felt hurt.

qa.q: What did the observer do about it?
qa.a: The observer quietly told Miss Reddy what was seen, since it was repeated and three against one.

qa.q: How might Akash have seen his own teasing?
qa.a: He may have meant it as a joke, and he said so, but he may not have noticed how it landed until Jahnavi went quiet.

grounding: Teasing among friends can shift into mocking when one person cannot laugh along, and watching the target's face and repetition helps tell fun from unkind.

passage:
Monday. At lunch Jagdish called Preeti “Slowcoach” because she was last in the race. She laughed and said, “Watch out, I'll beat you next time.”

Wednesday. He said it again in front of the whole line. Preeti smiled thinly and didn't reply. A friend, Mira, glanced at her.

Friday. Jagdish said it a third time, louder, and others joined. Preeti's face went blank, and she walked away. Mira followed her, then said to Jagdish, “She's not laughing anymore.” Jagdish stopped. He looked at Preeti's back. “I didn't mean it that way,” he said. Mira told the teacher about the three days.

qa.q: How many days in the week did Jagdish tease Preeti?
qa.a: Three, on Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling on Friday when her face went blank, and how was that different from Monday?
qa.a: On Monday she laughed, but by Friday she went blank and walked away, which suggests she was hurt and no longer found it funny.

qa.q: What did Mira do that helped?
qa.a: Mira followed Preeti, told Jagdish that Preeti was not laughing anymore and told the teacher about the three days.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel after he stopped?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and a little ashamed, since he said he did not mean it that way.

grounding: Playful teasing became mocking when Preeti could not laugh along, across three days, and an adult was told about ongoing harm.

passage: The pouring rain kept everyone in the school hall, and only one football and one skipping rope were left. Samir wanted football, and Francis wanted skipping. They stood facing each other, arms folded. The bell would ring in ten minutes. Samir said, “What if you pick this one, and I pick the next?” Francis frowned. “Skipping first?” “Skipping first,” Samir said. “Then football after lunch.” Francis thought about it. “Okay, but you remember.” “I'll write it on my hand.” Samir scribbled “football after lunch” on his palm. Francis grinned and picked up the rope.

qa.q: What did Samir write on his palm?
qa.a: “Football after lunch.”

qa.q: How was Francis feeling when he first stood with folded arms, and what changed?
qa.a: Francis was resisting and wanted skipping, but hearing a fair trade made Francis willing to agree.

qa.q: Why did the compromise work for both children?
qa.a: Each got a turn, Francis was heard first, and Samir wrote the deal on his hand so it would be remembered.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt giving up his pick for the first turn?
qa.a: He may have felt a little disappointed but comfortable, since he knew his football turn was coming.

grounding: A child proposes turns, you pick this game and I pick the next, and compromise works when both feel heard and the deal is remembered.

passage: “You pick the game today, I pick tomorrow,” Anand told Disha in the living room, holding the two board games. Disha crossed her arms. “But I always pick second.” “Then let's flip a coin,” Anand said. Disha shook her head. “Coins make me lose.” Anand thought. “Okay. You pick today. I'll pick the next two days.” Disha's face relaxed. “Two days? That's fair.” “Deal,” said Anand. They shook hands. Their mother, folding clothes nearby, smiled. Disha picked the snake game. Anand set up the pieces. “Tomorrow it's mine,” he said, and Disha nodded.

qa.q: Which game did Disha pick?
qa.a: The snake game.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when she said she always picks second?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair and was holding her ground, which is why she crossed her arms.

qa.q: What made Anand's second offer work?
qa.a: He listened to her reason, dropped the coin and offered her today while he took the next two days, so she felt heard.

qa.q: How might their mother see the deal?
qa.a: She may be pleased they worked it out themselves, since she watched and smiled.

grounding: A child proposes turns, splitting days and trading choices, and compromise works when both feel heard and the deal is remembered.

passage: “Everyone else in my class is allowed a phone,” said Gopika at dinner. Her father put down his spoon. “Everyone? Every single one?” Gopika hesitated. “Well, most.” “How many exactly?” “Three, I think.” Her father nodded. “Thank you for being honest. What is your reason?” “I finished my homework, so I should be able to chat with friends.” Arnab, her brother, said, “That's a real reason.” Her father said, “It's a fair argument, but a phone at your age isn't something we're ready for yet. What about using my phone for half an hour on weekends?” Gopika thought. “Okay.”

qa.q: How many classmates did Gopika say had phones once she was asked exactly?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why did Gopika say everyone else was allowed a phone, and what changed when her father asked?
qa.a: She wanted to persuade him, but when asked she admitted it was only about three, so exaggeration gave way to honesty.

qa.q: How did Gopika's father respond well?
qa.a: He thanked her for being honest, took her reason seriously, and offered a limited alternative while explaining his limit.

qa.q: How might Arnab have seen the argument?
qa.a: He thought the reason about finishing homework was fair, so he probably wanted to support his sister.

grounding: A child argues everyone else is allowed and I finished my homework so, and the adult responds to the argument while noting limits.

passage: Last week I really wanted to stay up late for the cricket final. I told Mummy, “Everyone is allowed!” She said, “Everyone?” I admitted that only Siddharth was. Then I tried a different reason: “I finished my homework, so I've earned it.” This time she listened. She said it was a real point but that the match ended after ten and school was next day. She offered to record it for the morning. I was cross for a minute, but I saw her reasons. I remember thinking that a true reason worked better than saying everyone. Manoj.

qa.q: Who was the only person allowed to stay up late?
qa.a: Siddharth.

qa.q: Why did Mummy's reply to “Everyone is allowed” differ from her reply to the homework reason?
qa.a: The first sounded exaggerated, and only Siddharth was allowed, while the second was a real reason she could take seriously.

qa.q: What alternative did Mummy offer for the cricket final?
qa.a: She offered to record it so it could be watched in the morning, which respected the limit and the wish.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's parents see their son staying up late?
qa.a: They may have their own reasons and rules, and Manoj's request shows that families decide differently.

grounding: A child argues everyone else is allowed and I finished my homework so, and learns a real reason works better than an exaggeration.

passage: At the school gate in Bhopal, Pankaj's classmate Uma said, “Come on, everyone does it. Just skip the quiz. You have to decide right now!” Pankaj felt his stomach tighten. He asked, “What's the reason?” Uma shrugged. “Because it's fun.” Pankaj said, “Let me think about it.” He walked away and found Ms. Nair, the counsellor. He told her that Uma was pressing him to hide from the quiz, and that she also had asked him to keep it secret. Ms. Nair thanked him. “Taking time and telling me was the right thing.” Pankaj felt his shoulders drop.

qa.q: Who did Pankaj tell about the pressure?
qa.a: Ms. Nair, the counsellor.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when Uma said everyone does it, and how do you know?
qa.a: He felt pressured and uneasy, since his stomach tightened, and he asked for a reason and time to think.

qa.q: Which habit helped Pankaj most?
qa.a: Asking what the reason was, taking time to think and telling a trusted adult about the pressure and the secret.

qa.q: How might Uma see Pankaj's walking away?
qa.a: She may feel annoyed that he did not go along, or she may not have thought it through, since her only reason was that it was fun.

grounding: A child notices everyone does it and pressure to decide quickly, asks what the reason is, takes time and tells a trusted adult.

passage: From the back of the classroom I saw Sabina talk to Karthik at the desk. “Everyone in Class 7 is doing it,” she said. “You have to decide by the bell, or you'll miss out.” Karthik looked at his shoes, then said, “Why?” Sabina said, “Because everyone is.” He didn't answer for a bit. “I want to think,” he said. Sabina said, “You'll regret it!” Karthik took his bag and walked to the teacher's desk. I couldn't hear what he said, but he looked calmer afterwards. I don't know what she wanted, but his questions seemed sensible.

qa.q: Who did Karthik go to after Sabina's talk?
qa.a: The teacher, at the teacher's desk.

qa.q: What was Karthik probably feeling when Sabina told him to decide by the bell?
qa.a: He probably felt pressured and unsure, so he asked why and said he wanted to think.

qa.q: What habit did Karthik show that others can copy?
qa.a: He asked for the reason, took time to think and went to a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Sabina see Karthik's decision to walk away?
qa.a: She may feel frustrated or worried he would miss out, though the observer cannot know what she wanted.

grounding: A child notices the everyone does it appeal and pressure to decide quickly, asks the reason, takes time and goes to a trusted adult, seen by an observer.

passage: Saturday. I told Charu my biggest secret today: I'm scared of the dark, still, and I keep the hall light on at night. She didn't laugh. She said she sometimes checks under her bed. We giggled. Then she told me another secret, that her cousin scared her by saying he'd hide her shoes. I said, “That isn't okay, Charu, you should tell your mum.” She said she would think about it. I felt proud she trusted me. But Amma says some secrets are safe and some aren't; if a secret makes you feel scared, you tell a grown-up. So tonight I told Amma, and she rang Charu's mum straight away. Rekha.

qa.q: What does Charu sometimes check?
qa.a: Under her bed.

qa.q: Why did Rekha feel proud after the talk?
qa.a: Rekha felt proud that Charu trusted Rekha with a secret and did not laugh at the shared fear.

qa.q: What did Rekha say to Charu about the secret that made Charu scared?
qa.a: Rekha said it wasn't okay and Charu should tell her mum, because a secret that feels scary should be told to a grown-up.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt after sharing both secrets?
qa.a: Charu probably felt relieved and closer to a friend, though she was still unsure about telling her mum.

grounding: A child confides in a best friend, building trust, and learns that a secret that causes fear or harm should be told to a trusted adult.

passage: Under the mango tree at the edge of the field, Rehana whispered to Zainab, “I have not told anyone this. I failed my spelling test and hid the paper in my bag.” Zainab listened, then said, “I won't tell. But you might feel better if you show Ammi. She won't shout.” Rehana's lips trembled. “What if she does?” Zainab squeezed her hand. “I can come with you.” The two walked to Rehana's home in the afternoon sun. Rehana showed the paper. Her mother sighed, then hugged her. Zainab waited outside, smiling. Rehana called out, “Thank you for coming.”

qa.q: Where did the girls talk?
qa.a: Under the mango tree at the edge of the field.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she whispered her secret?
qa.a: She was worried and ashamed about the spelling test, which is why she hid it and her lips trembled when asked about her mother.

qa.q: What did Zainab do that helped Rehana?
qa.a: She kept the confidence, suggested showing Ammi and offered to walk with Rehana, so the secret was shared with a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Rehana's mother have felt on seeing the paper?
qa.a: She sighed, which may have been worry, then hugged her, so she seemed to care more about Rehana than the mark.

grounding: A child shares a secret with a best friend and is encouraged to tell a trusted adult.

passage: “Why is the goat in the yard?” asked Dolma's mother as she came in from the field. Dolma looked at her feet. “I did it because... the gate was open, and the goat looked hungry.” “Who left it open?” “I did,” said Dolma. Anirban, her neighbour's boy, popped his head over the wall. “She wanted to feed him our cabbage leaves.” Dolma's cheeks reddened. “That's true. I'm sorry. I thought it wouldn't matter.” Her mother waited a moment. “I hear that you wanted to help the goat. Next time, ask me first.” Dolma nodded and shut the gate.

qa.q: Who left the gate open?
qa.a: Dolma.

qa.q: What did Dolma mean by saying the goat looked hungry, and what else did she admit?
qa.a: It was a real reason, since she wanted to feed the goat, but it was mixed with an excuse until she admitted she left the gate open and thought it wouldn't matter.

qa.q: What did Dolma's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She waited, listened for the need behind the reason, and asked Dolma to ask her first next time.

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt after telling on Dolma?
qa.a: He may have felt he was helping tell the truth, or a bit awkward for exposing her, since he added it over the wall.

grounding: A child explains I did it because, mixing real reasons and excuses, and the adult listens for the need behind it.

passage: “Ines, why did you take the last biscuit?” asked Olga's teacher at break in Lisbon. Ines said, “I did it because I was hungry.” Olga, standing next to her, added, “She skipped breakfast.” The teacher paused. “Was that the only reason?” Ines rubbed her ear. “And... I didn't want Mateo to get it.” The teacher nodded. “Thank you for telling me both. I understand being hungry. Next time, ask me for a snack.” Ines said, “Okay.” Olga touched her arm. Later the teacher brought Ines a piece of fruit and said quietly, “Come to me anytime.”

qa.q: Which city was the school in?
qa.a: Lisbon.

qa.q: What did Ines's two reasons show about what she was feeling?
qa.a: She was really hungry, and she also felt some rivalry about Mateo, so one reason was true and one was less comfortable to admit.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that made honesty easier?
qa.a: The teacher asked if that was the only reason, thanked Ines for both, understood the hunger and offered a snack next time.

qa.q: How might Olga have felt while standing next to Ines?
qa.a: Olga probably felt protective of a friend, since Olga added that Ines skipped breakfast, and perhaps nervous about what would happen.

grounding: A child explains I did it because, mixing real reasons and other motives, and the adult listens for the need behind the explanation without treating every reason as proof of intent.

passage: On the rain-soaked bus to the science museum, the bus crawled through traffic and the windows fogged up. Siddharth told the whole back row, “I once saw a snake as long as this bus!” Pradeep laughed. “As long as this bus? Really?” “Okay, maybe as long as the aisle,” Siddharth grinned, waving both arms. “No, maybe as long as my arm.” The whole row was giggling now. Their teacher looked back and smiled. “That snake keeps getting shorter!” Siddharth said, “It was a tiny one, but it felt long.” Pradeep said, “I'd like to see that snake.” Everyone laughed.

qa.q: What did Siddharth claim to have seen that was as long as the bus?
qa.a: A snake.

qa.q: How was Siddharth feeling while shrinking the snake, and how can you tell there was no wish to deceive?
qa.a: Siddharth was cheerful and enjoying the joke, grinning and waving both arms while the row giggled, and admitted the snake was tiny.

qa.q: Why did the exaggeration work as a joke?
qa.a: Everyone in the row shared the joke and knew the snake was not really that long.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen Siddharth's story?
qa.a: The teacher smiled and joined in, so probably saw it as harmless fun on a slow, wet ride.

grounding: A child exaggerates a tall tale for effect, and it is play rather than lying when both sides share the joke.

passage: “I ate a million rotis at Nani's house,” Jatin told Ramesh at the kitchen table, patting his stomach. Ramesh raised an eyebrow. “A million?” “Well, about a thousand.” Ramesh snorted. “You'd be bigger than a house.” Jatin puffed out his cheeks. “I was the biggest boy in the whole world!” They both cracked up. Ramesh's mother, cutting an onion, said, “I only made six, and half of them fell on the floor.” Jatin laughed even harder. “Okay, maybe two.” Ramesh grinned. “Exaggerating is your best trick.” Jatin bowed in his chair.

qa.q: How many rotis did Ramesh's mother say she made?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: Why did Jatin keep changing the number of rotis?
qa.a: Jatin was playing with the truth for fun, enjoying the joke, and both children knew it was not real.

qa.q: What makes this exaggeration different from lying?
qa.a: Both boys share the joke and know it is not real, and Jatin quickly admits a smaller number.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's mother have seen the tall tale?
qa.a: She joined in with a joke of her own, so she probably enjoyed it as harmless play.

grounding: A child exaggerates for effect, I ate a million rotis, playing with truth while both sides share the joke.
